source.title: Emergent phases of superposition: from partial to full representation
source.authors: Li-Hao Guo; Yizhou Liu; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains and measures the toy model of superposition, varying width and feature statistics, and reports representation geometry and loss. It uses the same basic toy-model method and measurements while examining new width and data-statistics regimes.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites LLM findings from other work, but those are not results of this study and are not recorded as rows. Partial random-projection approximation predictions are reported alongside the trained-model results; rows below focus on outcomes the study states or measures. Hyperparameters and values used only to set plots or training are not treated as results.
record.test_reason: The study trains Elhage et al.'s ReLU toy model, with n=10000 sparse features and width m from 10 to 16384, and measures feature-vector norms, overlaps, the participation ratio r and loss. This directly tests toy-model superposition (V1) in a new large-n regime with equal importance. It also bears on capacity allocation (V2) through frequency-dependent leverage scores. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that increasing width drives a continuous transition from partial to full representation in Anthropic's toy model. The critical width grows as Ē log(n/Ē), set by balancing crosstalk against discarding error. Loss is linear in Ē and weakly width-dependent below m*, and roughly quadratic in Ē and ∝1/m above it. Non-uniform firing delays the transition and lowers loss because frequent features occupy more dimensions. They note that extension beyond this architecture is unverified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Anthropic toy-model architecture and measures feature-vector representations and reconstruction loss, but assigns equal importance in the uniform setup and systematically varies width, sparsity, activation-count variability, and firing-probability inequality.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on mean active-feature count, firing-probability inequality, and variance of the number of active features. The partial/full grouping ceases to apply at large power-law inequality.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss shifts from a feature-discarding floor (∝Ē/n, nearly width-independent) to ∝Ē²log(n/Ē)/(nm) above the critical width, matching a compressed-sensing-like bound.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the large-n toy model, loss scales inversely with width once all features are represented, and the critical width is m*∼Ē log(n/Ē).

record.problems: Evidence is limited to the toy model and its linear representation assumptions; extension to other architectures and losses is unverified. Most figures omit error bars, though selected settings use 10 seeds and report small seed-to-seed variability. The partial random-projection analysis uses a Gaussian crosstalk approximation that the authors say overestimates loss in finite-size cases. Non-uniformity analysis is reliable only as a trend for the stronger tested inequality, and the authors state the transition characterization fails at large inequality.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. LLM findings mentioned in the related-work and discussion sections are cited from other studies, not measured here.

untested.parts: Small-n polytope or antipodal geometry; varied feature importance; the dense regime where Elhage find no superposition (all tests here have Ē/n≪1, where the paper shows non-superposition is never optimal).
Neuron-level polysemanticity (the hidden layer has no privileged basis); allocation by feature importance rather than by firing frequency.
Not tested. LLM results are only cited from other work.
Not tested. No SAEs are trained.
Not tested. Features are 1-D vectors by construction.

missing.what: Effect of activation-strength variance σv: m* decreases and loss increases as σv grows.
Crosstalk-noise geometry: the trained equal-norm frame gives negatively skewed, non-Gaussian crosstalk at larger m/n; skewness vanishes as m/n→0.
In trained models with non-uniform features, each feature's summed squared overlap matches 1/h_i − 1 across all features.

record.verdict_notes: Importance is equal across all features; only frequency varies, so V2's importance-based allocation is not directly tested. The transition studied (partial→full representation) is distinct from Elhage's sparsity-driven onset of superposition. The paper argues superposition is present at all tested widths in this sparse regime. Most settings use a single seed; 10-seed checks show negligible variance.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests toy networks, not LLM representations; its results apply to its linear-embedding, ReLU toy model and tested firing-probability regimes.
It tests feature allocation under a width bottleneck, including firing-probability differences, but does not test whether this explains polysemantic neurons in trained networks.
No alternative causes of polysemantic neurons are tested.
No LLM activations, feature spread across neurons, or SAE recovery are measured; cited LLM results are from other work.
No SAE features are studied for completeness, stability, or canonical status.
Each input feature is represented by a single vector by the toy-model formulation; the study does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Varied width m and measured representation norms and participation ratio r.
rows.measure: Representation completeness r/n and distribution of feature-vector norms.
rows.value: At small m, norms separate into a near-zero group and an appreciable-norm group; at large m, all features have appreciable, nearly equal norms. As m increases, r/n reaches 1 continuously at the critical width m*.
rows.uncertainty: Seed-to-seed standard deviations were reported as too small to see in most figures; 10 seeds were used for selected settings.
rows.note: The paper calls the regimes partial representation and full representation; its definition of m* is the smallest width at which the norm distribution becomes unimodal.
rows.check: Observed for V1. For V2 it is only partial: features compete for capacity and some are discarded, but the represented features share dimensions rather than any receiving a dedicated one. The toy hidden layer has no neuron basis, so polysemantic neurons are not measured.

source_check.correct: Observed for V1; partial for V2. Limited width causes feature dropping and overlapping representation, but this uniform-importance experiment does not demonstrate preferential dedicated dimensions.
source_check.problem: One observed state overstates the result for V2.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Compared participation ratio r with width m across the width sweep.
rows.value: r/m is always greater than 1, including in the partial-representation regime.
rows.note: The authors use this result to state that partial representation still involves superposition.
rows.check: Should also link to V2. r/m>1 at every width means represented features always overlap and none gets a dedicated dimension. This qualifies V2's 'important features get dedicated dimensions'.

source_check.correct: Observed for V1; cannot_determine for V2's preferential dedicated allocation from this measure alone. r/m>1 establishes aggregate superposition, not that every represented feature overlaps or that none has a dedicated dimension.
source_check.problem: The aggregate participation ratio does not establish V2's feature-specific allocation claim.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured loss as width m increased.
rows.value: Loss decays slowly before the transition and approximately as 1/m after it; the curve bends around m*.
rows.uncertainty: Seed-to-seed standard deviations were reported as too small to see in most figures.
rows.note: The text describes the width dependence; plotted numerical values are not transcribed.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.size_stated: n = 10000 in the main figures; n varied from 1000 to 65536 in experiments
rows.operation_detail: Varied mean number of active features Ē and estimated the critical width m*.
rows.measure: Critical width m* for transition to full representation.
rows.value: m* increases with Ē; in the stated limit 1 ≪ Ē ≪ n, m* ∼ Ē log(n/Ē).
rows.note: The paper says the predicted scaling is consistent with the experimental phase boundary.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Varied Ē and compared loss in partial- and full-representation regimes.

conditions.value: one setting below and one above the transition in Figure 5b

rows.measure: Mean squared reconstruction loss L as a function of Ē.
rows.value: In partial representation, L grows approximately linearly with Ē; in full representation, it grows approximately quadratically up to a logarithmic correction. The stated asymptotic forms are L ≈ (Ē/n)(v̄² + σv²) below m* and L ≈ [2σv² Ē²/(nm)] log(n/Ē) above m*.
rows.note: The authors state that the asymptotic trends match the experiments.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Varied the power-law exponent ϵp of feature firing probabilities.
rows.measure: Critical width m* and reconstruction loss L.
rows.baseline: The uniform-probability case ϵp = 0 is the reference for the reported trend; exact baseline values are not stated.
rows.value: As ϵp increases, m* increases and L decreases.
rows.note: The text reports the directions of change; the plotted numerical values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Drop the V2 link. A shift in m* and in loss does not itself measure how capacity is allocated; R7 carries that.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured norms, biases, and leverage scores across features with unequal firing probabilities.
rows.measure: Feature leverage score hi, norm si, and bias bi as functions of pi.
rows.baseline: Uniform-feature solution at the same Ē, m, and n is shown as a reference in Figure 7b.
rows.value: For higher pi, hi increases, si decreases, and bi increases. The response signs match the perturbation analysis, while the predicted magnitudes are overestimated.
rows.note: The authors interpret hi as an effective number of hidden dimensions allocated to a feature.
rows.check: For V2: more frequent features get larger leverage scores h_i, i.e. more capacity. Measured h_i stay centred near m/n, so the extra share is graded, not a dedicated dimension. Importance (as opposed to frequency) was not varied.

source_check.correct: Observed adaptation for V1; partial for V2. Higher firing probability increases leverage score and bias and decreases norm. Appendix C.3.2 tests only full representation; leverage scores remain centered near m/n. This establishes graded allocation rather than the full dedicated-dimension account.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Equations 17–19; Figure 7; Appendix C.3.2; Figure 25.
source_check.problem: Observed overstates V2; firing-frequency allocation is demonstrated, but dedicated dimensions and neuron polysemanticity are not.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Varied the variance σE² of the number of simultaneously active features.
rows.measure: Transition persistence, critical width m*, and loss.
rows.value: The partial-to-full transition persists in the tested range; m* grows with σE. In the full-representation phase, loss grows approximately linearly with σE² at small σE² and somewhat nonlinearly at larger σE². In the partial phase, loss is insensitive to σE.
rows.note: The paper says that at sufficiently large σE the behavior may differ; when all features always fire together, one vector can represent their firing states.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured norm distributions under increasingly unequal power-law firing probabilities.
rows.measure: Bimodality of feature-vector norms and whether features divide into represented and unrepresented groups.
rows.value: The partial-to-full transition persists only for moderate ϵp. At large ϵp, for example ϵp = 2, the norm bands merge even at small m and features cannot be divided into represented and unrepresented groups.
rows.note: The authors report that the partial-representation description and the partial RP approximation no longer apply in this regime.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.size_stated: n features and width m; specific values not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared a configuration representing only m features with a constructed configuration that represents m + 1 features using an antipodal pair.
rows.measure: Loss difference between non-superposition and constructed superposition configurations.
rows.baseline: Non-superposition configuration representing only m features.
rows.value: The gain from representing one more feature is of order Ē/n, while the added interference loss is of order Ē²/n²; the paper concludes the non-superposition configuration is always suboptimal in this regime.
rows.note: This is an analytical comparison, not a separate trained-model measurement.
rows.check: This is an analytical derivation (Appendix A.1.1, Eq. 32–33), not a trained-model measurement, and it has no subject run. Keep it only as a theoretical comparator showing non-superposition is suboptimal when Ē/n≪1.

rows.subject: Equal-norm (EN) model
rows.size_stated: n = 10000 in the reported example; parameters varied
rows.stage_stated: trained with representation-vector norms constrained equal
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean and variance of cosine similarities between distinct representation vectors.
rows.measure: Mean and variance of cij for i ≠ j, compared with their theoretical lower bounds.
rows.baseline: The theoretical lower bounds for the mean and variance of cosine similarities.
rows.value: For all tested parameters, both the mean and variance reach their theoretical lower bounds; the authors describe the trained frame as nearly a tight frame.
rows.note: This constrained EN model does not exhibit the partial-to-full transition; it is used to examine the geometry of represented features.

relationships.condition: Uniform independent or exchangeable features, n=10000, sparse Ē (1–64), varied width
relationships.reason: More features than dimensions are stored overlapping (r/m>1). The width at which all features are represented rises with sparsity as Ē log(n/Ē), and the transition persists under activation-count variance. Equal-norm frames reach the Welch/tight-frame overlap bounds (R1–R5, R8, R11).
relationships.display_finding: More features than dimensions were stored overlapping (r/m>1), and the width needed to represent all features scaled as Ē log(n/Ē), so it depended on sparsity. The transition survived variance in the number of active features, and equal-norm frames reached the Welch and tight-frame overlap bounds.

source_check.condition: Uniform independent or exchangeable features, n=10000, sparse Ē (1–64), varied width
source_check.reason: R1–R5 and R8 establish overlapping representations and a sparsity-dependent completeness transition; R11 establishes near-tight-frame geometry in the constrained EN model. Critical width increases with active-feature count Ē, meaning less sparse inputs, rather than increasing sparsity.

relationships.reason: The partial-to-full transition persists, with m* rising and loss falling as ϵp grows (R6, R7).
relationships.display_finding: The partial-to-full transition persisted, with m* rising and loss falling as ϵp grew.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R6–R7 and Appendix C.3.1 show that the completeness transition persists under moderate non-uniformity, with increasing critical width and decreasing loss.

relationships.reason: The norm bands merge even at small width, so no clean represented/unrepresented transition exists (R9).
relationships.display_finding: The norm bands merged even at small width, leaving no clean transition between represented and unrepresented features.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R9 shows merged norm bands even at small width, invalidating the clean partial/full representation description in this condition.

relationships.condition: Toy model with unequal firing frequencies, m=1000, ϵp=0.2
relationships.reason: Features compete for limited width: more frequent features receive larger leverage scores (more effective dimensions), and rarer features are dropped first (R7, R1).
relationships.display_finding: With unequal firing frequencies, more frequent features received larger leverage scores, meaning more effective dimensions.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Toy model with unequal firing frequencies, m=1000, ϵp=0.2
source_check.reason: R7 supports frequency-dependent graded allocation, not V2's dedicated-dimension account. Appendix C.3.2 tests full representation, so feature dropping is not demonstrated in that condition; R1 instead uses uniform frequencies. Neuron polysemanticity remains untested.

relationships.condition: Large-n sparse regime, all widths tested
relationships.reason: Competition takes the form of discarding features and graded sharing, not dedicated dimensions. r/m>1 always and h_i stays near m/n (R1, R2, R7).
relationships.display_finding: Competition showed up as discarded features and graded sharing rather than dedicated dimensions. The ratio r/m always exceeded 1, and h_i stayed near m/n at every width tested.

source_check.reason: R1–R2 show dropping and aggregate superposition; R7 shows graded frequency-dependent allocation in the tested full-representation settings. These qualify the dedicated-dimension account, although r/m>1 alone cannot prove that no individual feature has a dedicated dimension.
